newsitem.title: CROATIA: SOCCER-NEWCASTLE CLASH BRINGS NEW LIFE TO ZAGREB.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-NEWCASTLE CLASH BRINGS NEW LIFE TO ZAGREB.

text.p: After six years of dire games and deserted stadiums, soccer fever has returned to Zagreb with the Croatian champions setting their sights on returning to Europe's top flight.
Last week a capacity crowd of 35,000 watched Croatia Zagreb beat their greatest rivals Partizan Belgrade 5-0 in the first qualifying round of the European Cup.
The match, undoubtedly fuelled by political animosity, represented a festival of football unseen in Zagreb since the break up of communist Yugoslavia in 1991.
The club, players and fans are now concentrating on Newcastle -- the final obstacle barring Zagreb from Europe's lucrative and glamorous Champions' League.
The victory over Partizan has lifted spirits to such an extent that Croatian sports reporters have descended in droves on the northern English city on fact-finding missions.
"One can play with the English," declared one of the "experts" engaged by daily Vjesnik's sports pages.
Zagreb's political weekly Globus meanwhile gave heart to its readers with a depiction of the English league runners-up as "Newcastle -- the club that lost its stars."
Newcastle's problems in attack following the recent ankle injury to England captain Alan Shearer and the sale of striker Les Ferdinand to Tottenham are well documented.
However, Croatians also cite tradition to back their claim that they have a chance against the wealthy "Magpies".

Zagreb's greatest international success -- while the team competed under their former name Dinamo -- came 30 years ago when they beat another northern English club, Leeds, in the finals of the Fairs Cup, forerunner of the UEFA Cup.
But the 1967 success was followed by three decades of drought, as arguably the most popular Croatian club won just one Yugoslav championship and no international prizes.

After the break up of the Yugoslav league, dominated by Belgrade clubs Red Star and Partizan, Croatia lost their key players, including captain Zvonimir Boban who moved to AC Milan and Davor Suker who joined Spain's Seville.

The poor quality of the Croatian league, where Hajduk Split is Croatia's only serious rival, reduced the average number of spectators attending Sunday matches at Zagreb's Maksimir stadium to a few hundred per game.
Even winning back-to-back the league and cup double in 1996 and 1997 did not boost interest in the game because of a row between the fans and the club's management about its renaming.

After winning independence, the country's autocratic President Franjo Tudjman changed the club's name Dinamo, which sounded too communist to him, into the more appropriate Croatia, to the outrage of most supporters.

The most fervent fans, called the "Bad Blue Boys", still come to games bearing "Dinamo" emblems -- a small "d" on a blue flag -- and sing a punk rock anthem Sacred Name Dinamo to the embarrassment of the establishment.
But relations seemed to be easing somewhat as the club, under Tudjman's influence and apparently with state funds, embarked on an ambitious plan to build a "European" club.

Apart from buying just about every player worth buying on the depleted domestic market, the club has brought Robert Prosinecki back from Spain where he had an unsuccessful spell with Real Madrid and Barcelona.
Prosinecki was a member of the Croatian squad that reached the quarter-finals of the Euro '96 competition in England.

He was born in Zagreb and first joined Dinamo, but was quickly sold at the age of 18 to arch-rivals Red Star in the late 1980s in one of the affairs, spiced with ethnic disputes, that shook the Yugoslav soccer scene in its dying days.
It was precisely Prosinecki's technical brilliance and international experience in midfield that destroyed Partizan Belgrade's defence last week.

Croatia intend to build their revival around him and talented young players such as midfielder Silvio Maric and defender Dario Simic, who are both reportedly being chased by some of the biggest European clubs.
